cf.title: Soft DROP TABLE, recoverable drops for PostgreSQL

input.subject: [DESIGN] Soft DROP TABLE, recoverable drops for PostgreSQL

verdict_reasoning: The review stops at level 1b on already-exists-1. The patch touches only contrib and doc wiring and builds with PGXS, so the same code works as an outside extension. Message #6 asked why it must be in contrib and has no direct answer. The goal of recoverable drops is not in dispute, and the level 2 objections that survived were not evaluated.

brief.title: Contrib pgtrashcan: recoverable drop table via a reserved schema
brief.problem: An accidental drop table, often from automation run against the wrong cluster, destroys data that can only come back through point-in-time recovery or a logical restore. The author wants a lighter first line of recovery for operators, like Oracle's recycle bin or Snowflake's UNDROP TABLE.
brief.proposed_design: A new contrib extension, forked from Peter Eisentraut's 2014 pgtrashcan, uses a ProcessUtility hook to turn drop table into a move to a reserved pgtrashcan schema under an OID-derived name. A protected catalog records each dropped table, and SQL functions list, restore, and purge entries. Foreign keys, triggers, views, rules and RLS policies are dropped, and their definitions are kept as JSONB for manual rebuild.
user_visible_surface: New contrib extension pgtrashcan; needs shared_preload_libraries and CREATE EXTENSION in each database.
Reserved schema pgtrashcan with catalog table pgtrashcan._trash_catalog, holding original name, schema, OID, drop time, dropped_by and JSONB metadata.
SQL functions pgtrashcan_list_dropped(), pgtrashcan_restore() by name or OID, and pgtrashcan_purge().
GUC pgtrashcan.enabled (USERSET, default on) to opt out per session; GUC pgtrashcan.internal_operation (SUSET) for internal use.
Changed DROP TABLE behaviour; on restore, NOTICE messages emit the captured definitions of dropped dependent objects.
author_claims: Recovery from point-in-time recovery or backup is too heavy when an operator wants a table back minutes later.
Oracle, Db2 and Snowflake offer similar recovery, which shows a common need.
Indexes, TOAST and owned sequences move with the table and come back on restore.
The OID-derived name keeps several drops of the same table name apart and never hits NAMEDATALEN truncation.
A 58-test regression suite covers the extension.
brief.thread_state: Zsolt Parragi, Andreas Karlsson, Amit Kapila and Álvaro Herrera asked why this is not an outside extension and noted that DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE, DROP OWNED and DROP EXTENSION bypass the hook. Amit's last message asks for a hook at the right level, such as in performDeletion, before going further, and the author has not answered it.
unclear: The author has not said why the extension must be in contrib instead of updating or forking pgtrashcan outside core.
The patch does not handle pg_dump and pg_upgrade for the reserved schema and the tables in it.
Soft-dropped tables stay in publications and keep RLS, and the author has not given a fix.
Nothing caps the time or space a table stays in the trash schema, and nothing purges it automatically.
The patch does not say what happens to locks, privileges and ownership of a table during the move and on restore.
The hook does not cover partitioned tables, temporary tables, foreign tables, TRUNCATE, or rewrites such as VACUUM FULL.

prior_attempts.title: Log LSN before table is dropped
prior_attempts.quote: What stops us from logging all the same inside object access hook defined by extension?
prior_attempts.reason: The visible messages do not show why the entry was returned with feedback. Reviewers asked for changes. Jim Jones found that temporary and unlogged tables also trigger the message. Kirill Reshke asked why an extension using an object access hook could not do the logging, and noted that the logged LSN can be earlier than the commit record of the drop.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 logged the LSN at DROP TABLE so the table could come back through point-in-time recovery. This proposal keeps the table in a reserved schema, so no point-in-time recovery is needed.

objections.title: Contrib placement adds nothing the external pgtrashcan cannot do
objections.failure_scenario: A committer commits contrib/pgtrashcan, a 343 KiB module that uses only the existing ProcessUtility_hook. From then on the project owns its behaviour across every DDL change, release after release. The same code could have shipped as an update to the external pgtrashcan, with no extra cost to core.
objections.argument: The patch touches only contrib and doc wiring, so every part of it already works as an external extension built with PGXS, as the README shows. Andreas asked in message #6 why it cannot update or fork the existing extension outside core, and that question has no answer. Amit in message #7 gives one reason for in-tree placement, coordinated review with core, but the patch does not handle pg_dump, publications or the other coupled areas he lists. A similar question about using an extension hook was raised for [P1].
objections.author_must_show: What does contrib placement give this module that a maintained external fork of pgtrashcan, built with PGXS on the same hook, cannot give?

precedents.title: Log LSN before table is dropped

critic.reasoning: The patch touches only contrib and doc wiring, and the README shows a PGXS build, so the same code works outside core. Message #6 has no direct answer, and message #10 confirms the coupled areas Amit named are not handled. [P1] must not be used as support.

other_surviving.title: Drop table ... cascade moves child tables that stock Postgres keeps
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user runs `drop table customers cascade` with the extension installed. Stock Postgres drops only the foreign key on `orders` and leaves `orders` in place. The extension moves `orders` into the pgtrashcan schema, so the application's next query on `orders` fails with "relation does not exist".
other_surviving.argument: The commit message says CASCADE "walks pg_depend and pg_constraint to move FK-dependent child tables into the trash schema atomically with the parent", and the README repeats it. In core, CASCADE removes the dependent constraint and never the referencing table. So the extension widens what DROP removes from the user's view, while the docs say it only makes drops recoverable. Message #10 lists the CASCADE handling as settled scope and does not mention this difference.
other_surviving.author_must_show: With the extension installed, does `drop table parent cascade` leave every FK-referencing table in its original schema, as stock Postgres does?

critic.reasoning: The commit message and README both say CASCADE moves FK-dependent child tables into the trash schema. Stock Postgres drops only the foreign key constraint and keeps the referencing table, and the thread does not discuss this difference.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Dump and restore of the trash schema has no defined behaviour
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An operator dumps a database that has trashed tables and restores it into a new cluster. The restore runs `create table` and `alter table ... owner to` in the pgtrashcan schema, which the hook blocks, or it loads the rows with OIDs that no longer match. Restore then fails, or later restores by OID pick the wrong table or nothing.
other_surviving.argument: Trashed tables are not extension members, so pg_dump emits them like normal tables. The protection trigger and hook described in the docs block DML on `_trash_catalog` and ALTER/RENAME in the schema. `orig_oid` and the `trash_$<oid>` names also do not survive a logical restore, so the uniqueness claim in message #1 holds only within one cluster. Amit raised pg_dump and pg_upgrade in message #7, and message #10 confirms they are not handled.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What does pg_dump emit for the pgtrashcan schema and `_trash_catalog`, and how does a restore into a new cluster keep restore-by-name and restore-by-OID working?

critic.reasoning: Message #10 confirms that pg_dump and pg_upgrade treatment of the reserved schema is not handled. Trashed tables are not extension members, so pg_dump emits them, and the proposal does not say what a restore does with them.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: The trash catalog and trashed tables leak into FOR ALL TABLES publications
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A cluster has a FOR ALL TABLES publication, and the operator installs pgtrashcan on the publisher only. The first DROP TABLE inserts a row into pgtrashcan._trash_catalog, and the apply worker on the subscriber stops because that relation does not exist there. Replication stays down until someone finds the cause in the subscriber log.
other_surviving.argument: pgtrashcan._trash_catalog is an ordinary user table in an extension schema, so FOR ALL TABLES publishes it with the trashed relations. If the subscriber has the extension too, the apply worker writes catalog rows that describe tables the subscriber never moved. Messages #4 and #10 agree that trashed tables stay in publications, but message #5 only promises to exclude them later. Neither message covers the catalog table, and the patch has no fix for either.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How are pgtrashcan._trash_catalog and the trashed tables kept out of FOR ALL TABLES and FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA publications, and what does a subscriber see on drop and on restore?

critic.reasoning: FOR ALL TABLES publishes ordinary tables created by extensions, and an apply worker stops when the target relation is missing on the subscriber. Messages #5 and #10 accept that trashed tables stay published, and no message covers the catalog table.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Trashed relation files are kept with no limit and no automatic purge
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A partition-rotation job, the motivating case in message #1, drops a leaf partition of tens of GiB each day. With pgtrashcan.enabled on by default, no space is ever freed. The data volume fills weeks later, and the server stops accepting writes.
other_surviving.argument: DROP TABLE normally pairs the catalog delete with an unlink of heap, TOAST and index files at commit. This design removes that cleanup and moves it to a manual pgtrashcan_purge() call, with no size or time limit. Leaf partitions are plain tables, so the README's pass-through for partitioned tables does not protect rotation jobs. Scripts that drop and recreate tables to reclaim space break in the same way.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What bounds the disk space held by trashed relations, and how does a DROP-and-recreate workload get its space back without changes to every script?

critic.reasoning: The material shows no retention period, size limit or automatic purge, and the brief lists this as open. The per-session opt-out helps only scripts that someone edits, so an unchanged rotation job keeps its files.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Restore and purge have no per-table ownership check
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An operator grants EXECUTE on pgtrashcan_purge() so an application role can clean up after itself. That role then purges another team's dropped table, which it could never have dropped. The other team finds out when pgtrashcan_restore() fails during an incident.
other_surviving.argument: The docs describe the API as SECURITY DEFINER functions behind a protected catalog. Message #5 agrees only to revoke them from PUBLIC. That just moves the problem to whoever is granted EXECUTE. The material describes no rule tying restore or purge of an entry to the table owner, the dropped_by role, or the target schema's CREATE privilege, and restore can place a table in a schema other than the original.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which role may restore or purge a given trash entry, and which checks stop a grantee from acting on tables owned by others or restoring into another schema?

critic.reasoning: The visible docs describe SECURITY DEFINER functions and state no per-entry ownership rule, and message #5 commits only to revoking from PUBLIC. The function reference is truncated, so the full docs may contain such a rule.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Dropped tables stay readable and replicated under their old grants
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A DBA drops a table that holds personal data, believing access and replication have ended. Roles with existing SELECT grants can still read it in the pgtrashcan schema, and a FOR ALL TABLES publication keeps sending its changes to subscribers. Nobody notices until an audit.
other_surviving.argument: In message #10 the author confirms a soft-dropped table is a live relation and stays in publications, with no fix yet. The table keeps its ACL. Its RLS policies are dropped at DROP time, but the docs do not say whether relrowsecurity stays set. On restore, the table returns with its grants but without its policies until someone rebuilds them by hand from the NOTICE output, so rows the policies used to hide may be visible.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What happens to the ACL, the RLS flag and publication membership at drop time and at restore, and how is a restored table kept closed until its policies are rebuilt?

critic.reasoning: The README says RLS policies are dropped at drop time and rebuilt by hand after restore, and the proposal does not say what protects the rows in between. The publication part repeats replication-ondisk-1, and read access also needs USAGE on the pgtrashcan schema.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Statement-level hook cannot cover all drop paths, so contrib would freeze it
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An operator with pgtrashcan installed runs drop schema app cascade, or drop owned by a departing role, and the tables are destroyed for good. The operator finds out when the restore function lists nothing. Any later drop path added to core will also bypass the hook, and nothing will report it.
other_surviving.argument: Amit asked for the work to be built on a hook at the right level, such as performDeletion, before going further (message #11). The proposal has not answered that. The author agrees the gap exists and plans to divert deletions later (message #10). A contrib module ships the ProcessUtility design, the reserved schema and the catalog together, so changing the hook later means changing user-visible behaviour.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which core hook, existing or new, would let one interception point cover drop table, drop schema cascade, drop owned and drop extension, and could that hook be committed first?

critic.reasoning: Message #11 asks for a hook at the right level and has no reply; Amit doubts the DropStmt enumeration proposed in message #10. A new patch version that adds or extends a core hook could solve this, so it is fixable.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Hand-kept list of dependent object types will drift silently
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A later release adds a new kind of object that depends on a table. The capture code does not know it, so drop table removes it without recording its definition. The user restores the table and finds the object missing, with no NOTICE.
other_surviving.argument: The patch drops foreign keys, triggers, views, matviews, rules and RLS policies and records their DDL as JSONB (README hunk). That list must grow with every new dependent object type, and no test or build step fails when someone forgets. Publication membership is already outside the list (messages #4, #10).
other_surviving.author_must_show: How would a future patch that adds a new dependent object type be forced to update pgtrashcan, rather than being missed by the author and the reviewer?

critic.reasoning: The list of captured object types is fixed in the extension, and nothing fails when core adds a new type. An unknown object would more likely stay attached to the trashed table than be removed, as publication membership does today, which is still a silent gap.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: No reason given to move a 2014 out-of-tree extension into contrib
refuted.failure_scenario: The project ships contrib/pgtrashcan with a hook that covers only DROP TABLE. Later changes to dependency handling, publications or pg_dump must keep the module working, and committers carry that work. If users still lose tables through DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE, they file bugs against core.
refuted.argument: Messages #1 and #2 say the patch is a fork of pgtrashcan, which has lived outside core since 2014, and the proposal does not say what blocked that path. Andreas asked in message #6 why the features cannot go into the existing extension or a fork outside core, and Amit questioned core value in message #7; message #10 asks for contrib without answering either. [P1] faced the same question on a nearby drop-recovery idea: why an extension using a hook could not do it.
refuted.author_must_show: What does contrib give that an updated out-of-tree pgtrashcan cannot, and which users of the 2014 extension asked for it in core?

precedents.title: Log LSN before table is dropped

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which makes the same point with more concrete support from the patch. [P1] proposed a core log message and its recorded reason is not known, so it gives no support.

refuted.title: Default-on USERSET GUC changes what DROP TABLE means
refuted.failure_scenario: A nightly job drops large staging tables to free disk after the extension is installed. DROP succeeds, but no space comes back and nothing purges it, so the disk fills. The dropped tables also stay in FOR ALL TABLES publications and show up in information_schema.tables and `\dt pgtrashcan.*`, so new subscriptions and schema-diff tools see tables that do not exist on the other side.
refuted.argument: `pgtrashcan.enabled` defaults to on, and the extension changes DROP TABLE for every session in the database, so scripts and tools written for stock semantics change behaviour without opting in. The brief notes there is no retention cap or automatic purge. Message #5 accepts that keeping trashed tables in publications is "not acceptable" but gives no fix. A GUC that changes DDL semantics also leaves a script's behaviour dependent on session state the script cannot see.
refuted.author_must_show: How does a script written for stock DROP TABLE semantics keep its disk-space and catalog-visibility guarantees once the extension is installed?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-3 for disk space and replication-ondisk-1 for publications. The remaining point fails because the operator opts in through shared_preload_libraries and CREATE EXTENSION, and changing DROP TABLE is the stated purpose of that choice.

refuted.title: OID-derived trash names do not survive a logical dump and restore
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator moves a database to a new cluster with pg_dump. Trashed tables come back as live tables such as trash_$16385 under new OIDs, so orig_oid and restore-by-OID point at nothing. A later drop of a table that gets OID 16385 tries to create trash_$16385 and fails.
refuted.argument: The brief says the OID keeps names unique "across the cluster's lifetime", but OIDs are not kept by a logical restore, and the patch does not mark the catalog for pg_extension_config_dump. Message #10 confirms that pg_dump and pg_upgrade handling of the reserved schema is not addressed. In message #7, Amit lists that handling as a reason the feature needs care that evolves with core. The design ties identity to a value that does not survive the most common migration path.
refuted.author_must_show: What do pg_dump, restore, and pg_upgrade produce for the pgtrashcan schema, its catalog and the trashed tables, and how is the name-to-OID mapping kept valid afterward?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2. Its claim about pg_extension_config_dump also cannot be checked, because the material does not show the extension script.

refuted.title: Unbounded trash retention lets any table creator fill the disk
refuted.failure_scenario: A role with CREATE on a schema, or an ETL job that creates and drops staging tables, drops tables repeatedly. The trash grows with no cap and no automatic purge. If purge is revoked from PUBLIC as message #5 proposes, that role cannot reclaim the space, and the cluster runs out of disk.
refuted.argument: pgtrashcan.enabled defaults to on, so every drop keeps its files unless the session opts out. The proposal has no retention period, size limit or background purge. Revoking the API, as agreed in message #5, means only privileged roles can free space that unprivileged roles fill.
refuted.author_must_show: What bounds the space one role can hold in the trash, and how does a table owner without purge rights free the space its own drops consume?

critic.reasoning: A role that can create tables can already fill the disk without this extension, and pgtrashcan.enabled is USERSET, so that role can opt out. The remaining retention concern is a duplicate of replication-ondisk-3.

refuted.title: No reason given why this belongs in contrib, not outside core
refuted.failure_scenario: Core takes over a fork of an external 2014 extension. A change to dependency handling, publications or pg_dump then breaks a 343 KiB module, and the fix falls to a committer who never reviewed it. The external original keeps going separately, so users get two diverging pgtrashcan versions.
refuted.argument: Zsolt and Andreas asked why the features cannot go into the existing extension or into an outside fork (messages #4, #6). The author agreed the mechanism can live in an extension (message #5) but did not say why it must be in contrib. Amit's argument for in-tree, coupling to evolving subsystems (message #7), points to a core hook rather than a contrib module. In the precedent, reviewers asked the same question about a drop-recovery aid.
refuted.author_must_show: What does being in contrib give users or maintainers that an updated outside extension built on the same hooks cannot give?

precedents.title: Log LSN before table is dropped

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1. [P1] gives no support, because its recorded reason for being returned is not known.

refuted.title: Default-on trash keeps disk space with no retention limit
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA on a nearly full volume drops a large table to free space, and pgtrashcan.enabled defaults to on. The space is not released, and autovacuum and publications keep treating the table as live. The DBA finds out when the disk fills.
refuted.argument: The documentation sets pgtrashcan.enabled to on by default, at USERSET level. Purge happens only on request, and nothing caps age or size. The thread confirms that soft-dropped tables stay live relations (message #10). Oracle and Snowflake, cited in message #1, both bound how long they keep dropped tables.
refuted.author_must_show: What bounds the space and time a soft-dropped table holds, and how does an operator free space at once in an emergency?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-3, which states the same retention problem with the thread's own partition-rotation case.

refuted.title: The core gap is a deletion hook, which this patch does not add
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator runs DROP SCHEMA app CASCADE or DROP OWNED BY with pgtrashcan installed and expects recovery. The tables go through performMultipleDeletions and are removed for good. The operator finds out only when pgtrashcan_list_dropped() shows nothing.
refuted.argument: Message #10 shows that all drop paths meet in performMultipleDeletions. Message #9 and message #11 suggest a hook there, or an extended existing hook. A small hook at that point would let the external extension cover every path, so contrib would gain little. Message #11 asks the module to be built on such a hook before going further, and the proposal does not answer.
refuted.author_must_show: Would a general hook in the deletion machinery let the existing external pgtrashcan cover all drop paths, and if so, why add a contrib module too?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1 for the missing deletion hook, and of already-exists-1 for the point that contrib adds little.

refuted.title: No demand shown for contrib over the existing external extension
refuted.failure_scenario: The module goes into contrib on the strength of two anecdotes, so committers must keep its hook working as dependency handling, publications and pg_dump change. Few sites set shared_preload_libraries and run CREATE EXTENSION in every database. The project carries the upkeep for each release while the external pgtrashcan, which the author could update or fork, already serves the same group.
refuted.argument: The evidence is two incidents the author saw in message #1 and the fact that Oracle, Db2 and Snowflake have a similar feature. Nothing shows users of the 2014 pgtrashcan asking for it to be maintained, and no -general or -bugs reports are cited. Message #6 asked why the work cannot live outside core, and message #7 doubts the use cases justify core inclusion. Message #10 argues for contrib on scope and footprint, which shows why the module is small, not that enough users want it shipped with Postgres.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users run the external pgtrashcan or a fork today, and what stops them from getting this version outside core?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1 on why contrib is needed over an outside extension. On demand for the feature, the rubric counts other databases that have it as evidence, and Amit calls the use cases reasonable in message #7.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: Trashed relation files stay on disk until a manual purge, and pg_upgrade of the reserved schema is not handled.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: Soft-dropped tables stay in publications, and pgtrashcan._trash_catalog is an ordinary table that FOR ALL TABLES publishes.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: The extension adds the reserved pgtrashcan schema and the protected table pgtrashcan._trash_catalog, keyed by OID-derived names.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The module depends on ProcessUtility_hook, and message #11 asks for a hook in the deletion code instead.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: DROP TABLE becomes a move to another schema, and CASCADE also moves FK-referencing tables.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The patch adds pgtrashcan.enabled (USERSET, default on) and pgtrashcan.internal_operation (SUSET).

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: pg_dump emits trashed tables as normal tables, and message #10 confirms the patch does not handle this.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: Restore and purge are SECURITY DEFINER functions, and trashed tables keep their grants while their RLS policies are dropped.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A 343.6 KB contrib module must follow every change to drop paths, dependent object types, publications and pg_dump.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: The module is a fork of an outside extension and uses only an existing hook, so it can stay outside core.

questions: What does contrib placement give this module that a maintained outside fork of pgtrashcan, built with PGXS on the same hook, cannot give?
Which core hook, existing or new, would let one interception point cover drop table, drop schema cascade, drop owned and drop extension, and could it be committed first?
What bounds the disk space and time held by trashed relations when a rotation job drops tables without setting pgtrashcan.enabled to off?
How are pgtrashcan._trash_catalog and the trashed tables kept out of FOR ALL TABLES publications, and what does pg_dump emit for them?
Which role may restore or purge a given trash entry, and what keeps a restored table closed until its RLS policies are rebuilt?

committability.owner_note: The owner would need to know the dependency and deletion code (performDeletion), and also logical replication and pg_dump. Reviewers in the thread asked design questions, but none has offered to take the patch.
committability.liability: The owner signs for changed DROP TABLE behaviour in a shipped module, for as long as contrib carries it. Every new drop path or dependent object type needs a matching change, and nothing fails when one is missed.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted the patch, answered reviewers in messages #5 and #10, and moved the entry to the next CommitFest on 2026-10-15. Message #11 has no reply yet.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: A concrete need that only in-tree placement meets would change the answer, for example a new core deletion hook that the module depends on and tests. Reports from users of the outside pgtrashcan who cannot get this version outside core would also count. The level 2 design points still need answers after that.

priority.reason: Accidental drops are a real operator problem, and message #1 cites similar features in Oracle, Db2 and Snowflake. The 343.6 KB patch misses DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE and DROP OWNED, and the thread asks for a hook at the right level and a reason for contrib before review continues.

provisional_note: The code was not read, and the function reference in pgtrashcan.sgml is truncated. Lock handling during the move, search_path in the SECURITY DEFINER functions, and any per-entry privilege checks could not be judged.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Log LSN before table is dropped
precedents_retrieved.authors: Andrey Borodin (x4m), Nik Samokhvalov (nikolay), Kirk Wolak (kirkw)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch writes a LOG message with the current WAL insert LSN when DROP TABLE acquires its lock, so an accidentally dropped table can be restored by point-in-time recovery to that LSN. The authors asked whether to do the same for DROP DATABASE, TRUNCATE, and DELETE or UPDATE without a WHERE clause.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why the entry was returned with feedback. Reviewers asked for changes. Jim Jones found that temporary and unlogged tables also trigger the message. Kirill Reshke asked why an extension using an object access hook could not do the logging, and noted that the logged LSN can be earlier than the commit record of the drop.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
What stops us from logging all the same inside object
access hook defined by extension?

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve recovery performance of dropping database having many tablespaces
precedents_retrieved.summary: DROP DATABASE would write one XLOG_DBASE_DROP record listing all tablespaces of the database, instead of one record per tablespace. On a standby, replay would then scan shared_buffers once, not once per tablespace.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers supported the idea and found the patch logically correct, but asked for performance numbers that show the recovery gain. One tester saw no difference with the patch, and Simon Riggs asked to rename tablespace_num to ntablespaces. The author did not respond for about two and a half months while the patch waited on author, so Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This was a couple of months ago, and nothing has happened since with the
patch waiting on author, so the patch is marked as returned with
feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add callback table access method to reset filenode when dropping relation
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a relation_reset_filenode callback to the table access method interface, called from heap_drop_with_catalog when a table is dropped, as the counterpart of relation_set_new_filenode. The goal was to let table AMs with non-file storage, such as an in-memory table, clean up their storage on DROP TABLE.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Heikki Linnakangas pointed out that dropping storage must happen at commit or abort and be redone from the commit record during WAL replay, which cannot run AM-specific code. A callback at drop time, or xact callbacks run at commit, therefore cannot drop storage correctly. Heikki suggested using smgrGetPendingDeletes() instead. The patch then stopped applying, the author did not reply when asked whether he was waiting for feedback, and the entry was marked Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't think implementing dropping relation data at-commit/rollback using
xact callbacks can be correct. The dropping needs to be integrated with the
commit / abort records, so it is redone during crash recovery - that's not
possible with xact callbacks.

precedents_retrieved.title: Prevent ALTER TABLE DROP NOT NULL on child tables if parent column has it
precedents_retrieved.summary: Prevent ALTER TABLE ... DROP NOT NULL on a child table when the same column in a parent table is marked NOT NULL, so that the constraint can only be dropped from the parent. The patch added a function in pg_inherits.c to list a relation's parents and a new index on pg_inherits.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane said the approach was wrong because it does not help decide whether to propagate DROP NOT NULL from a parent to its children, and pointed to the earlier plan of storing NOT NULL constraints in pg_constraint with inheritance counts as CHECK constraints do. After Vitaly Burovoy reported that he was writing such a patch, which already forbids dropping inherited NOT NULLs, the author withdrew his proposal in favour of that work.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This doesn't sound like the right approach; in particular, it won't really
help for deciding whether to propagate a DROP NOT NULL on a parent rel to
its children.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix ALTER TABLE DROP EXPRESSION with ONLY option
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... DROP EXPRESSION work on inheritance trees with more than one level, where it now fails with "must be applied to child tables too". It adds a `!recursing` check in ATPrepDropExpression() so the ONLY check runs only for the table named in the command.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Peter Eisentraut asked why tablecmds.c passes recurse = false when recursing, and suggested a more consistent use of the two flags would make the existing code work. Tom Lane said that if the flags matter here, DROP EXPRESSION should not use ATSimpleRecursion. The author replied in December 2025 that v3 is correct, and no later reply appears before the entry was returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Call RelationDropStorage() for broader range of object drops.
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Robert Haas, Alvaro Herrera, Alexander Korotkov
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes heap_drop_with_catalog() to call RelationDropStorage() for any relation with a valid relfilenode, instead of skipping views, composite types, foreign tables and partitioned tables. The goal was to let FDWs such as cstore_fdw keep data in Postgres storage without custom cleanup code for DROP EXTENSION.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas argued that a foreign table's relfilenode has no file behind it, so it is not guaranteed to be unique, and a table rewritten by CLUSTER or VACUUM FULL could get the same relfilenode. Dropping the foreign table would then delete that table's storage, which affects postgres_fdw and other FDWs that create no files. Alvaro Herrera and Alexander Korotkov also said FDWs are not the right interface for a storage format, and that pluggable storage is the right fix.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So I
think it might be possible for a table that gets rewritten by CLUSTER
or VACUUM FULL to end up with the same relfilenode that was previously
assigned to a foreign table; dropping the foreign table would then
nuke the other relation's storage.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow reads to proceed during FK/trigger drops by reducing relation-level lock from AccessExclusive to ShareRowExclusive
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lowers the relation-level lock taken while dropping foreign key constraints and their RI triggers from AccessExclusiveLock to ShareRowExclusiveLock, so that SELECTs on the other table keep running. A revised patch narrowed the change to RI action triggers on the referenced table and kept AccessExclusiveLock elsewhere.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane said the change is unsafe for FK removal, because the planner may have built query plans that rely on the constraint holding, as the comment in AlterTableGetLockLevel explains. He also noted that the first patch lowered the lock for other constraint types, and that dropping a unique constraint can also break existing plans. The author posted a narrower patch, but no one replied to it, and the visible messages do not show why it was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Adding a foreign key can (and I think does) take a lesser lock,
because the additional constraint won't invalidate any proofs the
optimizer may have made beforehand.  But dropping one seems
problematic.

precedents_retrieved.title: Close race in DROP TABLESPACE on Windows
precedents_retrieved.summary: On Windows, DROP TABLESPACE can fail with "tablespace is not empty" because another backend still holds an open descriptor on an unlinked file, which Windows keeps in the directory. Noah Misch proposed that DROP TABLESPACE wait for other backends to close such files, for example by polling with a new wait_unlinked_files() function.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No code was written. Noah Misch recorded the fix as a TODO and changed the regression test to use RESET ROLE instead of \c -, so only one backend is involved. Amit Kapila said the wait could last until the other backend runs another command. Alternatives (a catchup interrupt, renaming files to the tablespace top-level directory before unlink) were left for whoever decides to work on the issue.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think we can discuss further about which approach is better, once someone decides to work on this issue.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
precedents_retrieved.authors: Michael Paquier, Alexander Korotkov, Simon Riggs
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
Reverted commit(s): Fix handling of orphaned 2PC files in the future at recovery; Fix failures with incorrect epoch handling for 2PC files at recovery; Make use FullTransactionId in 2PC filenames; Speedup 2PC recovery by skipping two phase state files in normal path
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 8f67f994e8ea (down to v13) and c3de0f9eed38 (down to
v17), as these are proving to not be completely correct regarding two
aspects:
- In v17 and newer branches, c3de0f9eed38's check for epoch handling is
incorrect, and does not correctly handle frozen epochs.  A logic closer
to widen_snapshot_xid() should be used.  The 2PC code should try to
integrate deeper with FullTransactionIds, 5a1dfde8334b being not enough.
- In v13 and newer branches, 8f67f994e8ea is a workaround for the real
issue, which is that we should not attempt CLOG lookups without reaching
consistency.  This exists since 728bd991c3c4, and this is reachable with
ProcessTwoPhaseBuffer() called by restoreTwoPhaseData() at the beginning
of recovery.

Per discussion with Noah Misch.

roaster_notes.note: The thread names pgtrashcan (2014, outside core) as the earlier form of this idea in messages #1 and #2. The material gives no reason why that extension stayed out of core.
Objections listed; desirability and the hook-placement question raised in message #11 are covered by other angles.

The design adds no WAL records, on-disk format, wire messages or core ABI. Physical standbys replay ordinary catalog changes, so the objections cover only logical replication, dump and restore, and space reclamation.
Objections focus on privileges and exposure only. Without the code, I could not check search_path handling in the SECURITY DEFINER functions or in the generated DDL strings.
Two objections raised from the already-exists angle.

Demand for undoing accidental drops is plausible, given the incidents in message #1 and similar features in other systems. What the material lacks is evidence that users want this module in contrib rather than as an external extension.
